definition: Pluralism means the coexistence and acceptance of many different groups, beliefs, or traditions.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pluralism. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pluralism should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The choir director ran the season on cheerful pluralism, letting gospel, plainchant, and pop share one program without ranking them.
Tolerance puts up with difference and stops there, well short of pluralism.
Acceptance goes further than tolerance, welcoming difference rather than enduring it, but pluralism goes further still: it builds the whole arrangement around many groups living side by side.

Multiculturalism is about many cultures specifically — cuisines, languages, and holidays sharing one society. Pluralism is broader and more structural: many groups, beliefs, or traditions coexisting by accepted arrangement, cultures included but also faiths, parties, and schools of law. Multiculturalism names the mix; pluralism names the principle that protects it.

Inclusiveness is the habit of welcoming everyone in — an attitude a person or club can carry with no system behind it. Pluralism is the system itself: a standing arrangement in which different groups keep their own shape side by side. A host can be inclusive; pluralism takes a whole design.

When the new nation wrote its constitution, the drafters faced three living systems of law — civil courts in the cities, religious courts in the north, and village councils everywhere else.
Rather than crown one, the charter recognized all three, each supreme in its own sphere, with a mixed bench to referee the borders between them.
Foreign observers called the design pluralism in its purest form.

Pluralism goes beyond tolerance: tolerance puts up with difference, while pluralism means the coexistence and acceptance of many groups, beliefs, or traditions — difference designed in, not merely endured.
It names a standing arrangement, which is why constitutions and charters are where the word does its work.
Pluralism is the word of charters, courts, and civics classes — it names a standing arrangement, not a mood.
Its neighbor in this unit is cosmopolitan: a cosmopolitan person or city is at ease among many cultures, while pluralism is the principle that lets those cultures keep their own shape side by side.
For the simple fact of mixture, variety is enough.

When Ridgeline College rewrote its student government, the drafters aimed for pluralism rather than simple majority rule.
The new senate reserved seats for religious clubs, political societies, athletic teams, and the arts council, and no bloc could dissolve another.
Budget week made the design visible: the chess club and the debate union argued loudly, yet each knew its seat was safe.
A visiting reporter asked why the college put up with so much noisy disagreement.
The senate president shrugged: the noise was the point — the charter was built so that different groups could keep their own shape and still share one room.
